newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh sees prospects in South Asia triangle.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh sees prospects in South Asia triangle.

text.p: Bangladesh Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria said on Sunday the new South Asia Development Triangle (SADT) had tremendous opportunities for development.

"The concept developed by the World Bank is extremely important for a region needing quick co-ordination (for development) so that potential beneficiaries can reap the fruits," he told a workshop on the SADT in Dhaka.
World Bank officials said the SADT region encompasses an area of about 1.2 million square km with about 500 million people.
It includes Bangladesh, Bhutan, Nepal and India's Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and northeastern states.
The bank officials said more such workshops would be organised in other member countries before the SADT region would be formally launched.

Pierre Landell-Mills, head of the World Bank mission in Bangladesh, said "this region is one of the poorest areas in the world, with more than two-thirds of the population living on less than $1 a day. By 2025, the population of the SADT region is expected to exceed one billion.

"To alleviate widespread poverty in the SADT region, and to enable it to participate fully in the economic growth happening in Asia, there is a need for long-term vision in development and sustainable management of the region's resources."
The World Bank noted that the region was richly endowed with natural resources.

"In terms of water per unit of land, the Ganges-Brahmaptra-Meghna basin (corresponding roughly to the SADT region) is second only to the Amazon. There are also huge reserves of coal and natural gas and an underutilized potential for hydropower.
"It is strategically located at the hub of the Bay of Bengal, forming a potentially convenient link between East Asian, Central Asian, and West European countries."

Maritta Koch-Weser, chief of the World Bank's Asia Environment Division, said: "Within the region, there are several critical issues primarily of a trans-boundary nature that cannot be addressed within a national setting."
She cited flooding, water storage and hydro-power generation as three examples.
How the triangle would fit within the framework of South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC), however, remains to be seen.

The SAARC groups Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal, Maldives, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. But its success over more than a decade has been minimal because of rivalries between its biggest partners India and Pakistan over Kashmir, officials say.
Meanwhile, a recent agreement among India, Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan to form a sub-regional economic cooperation bloc has drawn severe criticism from Bangladesh's opposition political parties.
Diplomatic sources said Pakistan had also has expressed its reservation about the sub-regional bloc.
"We need political consensus before executing such type of cooperation. We are suffering from mistrust and distrust," former minister Sirajul Hossain Khan told the workshop.
